::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What this lesson is for

In the first lesson you learned to press **Run** and read the answer. Before you start asking
questions of your data — *which district landed the most fish? how much tilapia last month?* — it helps to
know **how your data is arranged**: what one line in the table stands for, how the lines fit together,
and what each column is telling you.

That is all this lesson does. Once the shape of the data is clear, the next lessons will make sense. Go
slowly, press **Run** on each box, and remember: **you cannot break anything.**
:::

## Where your data comes from

Your data does not appear from nowhere. Every time an enumerator meets a fisher coming back to a
landing site, they fill in a short survey: the date, the landing site, the boat and gear used, how many
people fished, and **what was caught**.

All of those surveys, from every landing site, are collected into **one big table**. That table is your
data. Reading it is simply reading those survey records, stacked one on top of another.

A table has two simple parts:

- a **row** is one line going across — one record;
- a **column** is one heading going down — one piece of information that was recorded, like the date or the weight.

The rest of this lesson is about what the rows and columns in *your* table mean.

## A small example to look at

It is easier to see the shape on a small table first. Here is a made-up example — just **two fishing
trips**, with each trip shown in its **own colour**.

```{=html}
<style>
/* colour rows by trip — scoped to row classes (Quarto re-renders the table and drops
   table-level classes, but keeps row classes); !important beats Bootstrap's cell bg. */
tr.trip1 td { background: #dbe9f6 !important; }   /* trip_1 — blue  */
tr.trip2 td { background: #fdebd0 !important; }   /* trip_2 — amber */
p.legend span { display:inline-block; width:.9em; height:.9em; vertical-align:middle; border:1px solid #888; margin-right:.3em; }
</style>

<table class="table">
  <thead><tr><th>survey_id</th><th>trip_id</th><th>landing_date</th><th>gaul_2_name</th><th>gear</th><th>catch_taxon</th><th>catch_kg</th><th>n_catch</th><th>tot_catch_kg</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="trip1"><td>survey_1</td><td>trip_1</td><td>2024-01-05</td><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>Tilapia</td><td>12</td><td>3</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="trip1"><td>survey_1</td><td>trip_1</td><td>2024-01-05</td><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>Snapper</td><td>5</td><td>3</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="trip1"><td>survey_1</td><td>trip_1</td><td>2024-01-05</td><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>Octopus</td><td>3</td><td>3</td><td>20</td></tr>
    <tr class="trip2"><td>survey_2</td><td>trip_2</td><td>2024-01-06</td><td>Vanga</td><td>gillnet</td><td>Tilapia</td><td>8</td><td>2</td><td>14</td></tr>
    <tr class="trip2"><td>survey_2</td><td>trip_2</td><td>2024-01-06</td><td>Vanga</td><td>gillnet</td><td>Snapper</td><td>6</td><td>2</td><td>14</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="legend"><span style="background:#dbe9f6"></span> Trip 1 &nbsp;&nbsp; <span style="background:#fdebd0"></span> Trip 2</p>
```

Take a moment to read it. Notice that some things **repeat** down the table while others **change** on
every line. We will come back to that, because it is the key to understanding your data.

The headings are the **real headings from your own data**. Here is that same little table inside R, so we
can work with it. This box runs on its own when the page opens — you do not have to do anything yet.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**If nothing happens at first,** R is still waking up — it can take a minute the first time, on a slow
connection. A small **spinning circle** on the box means it is working. Wait for it to stop.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
# The same five rows as the coloured table above.
example <- data.frame(
  survey_id    = c("survey_1", "survey_1", "survey_1", "survey_2", "survey_2"),
  trip_id      = c("trip_1", "trip_1", "trip_1", "trip_2", "trip_2"),
  landing_date = c("2024-01-05", "2024-01-05", "2024-01-05", "2024-01-06", "2024-01-06"),
  gaul_2_name  = c("Shimoni", "Shimoni", "Shimoni", "Vanga", "Vanga"),
  gear         = c("hand line", "hand line", "hand line", "gillnet", "gillnet"),
  catch_taxon  = c("Tilapia", "Snapper", "Octopus", "Tilapia", "Snapper"),
  catch_kg     = c(12, 5, 3, 8, 6),
  n_catch      = c(3, 3, 3, 2, 2),
  tot_catch_kg = c(20, 20, 20, 14, 14)
)

example
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** the same **5 rows** as the coloured table. You can slide it sideways to see all
the columns.
:::

## What one row means

Look at the very first line. It is one **catch**: *Tilapia, 12 kg*. The second line is another catch:
*Snapper, 5 kg*.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Each row is one catch — one kind of fish from one trip.**
:::

This is the first thing to hold on to. A row is **not** a whole trip, and it is **not** one fisher. It
is one *kind of fish* that was recorded. So if a single trip brought back three kinds of fish, that
trip fills **three rows**.

## How the rows fit into trips

You may have noticed something that confuses almost everyone at first: the same district, the same date and
the same `trip_id` appear on several lines. Nothing is wrong — this is exactly how the data is meant to
look.

The reason is simple: **one fishing trip usually brings back more than one kind of fish.** Each trip is
given an identity code, **`trip_id`** (and `survey_id`, the survey it came from). Every kind of fish
from that trip gets its own row, and they all carry the **same** `trip_id`. That shared code is how you
know which rows belong to the same trip.

In the example, `trip_1` brought back three kinds of fish, so it fills three rows. `trip_2` brought back
two, so it fills two rows. Here is that first trip drawn as a picture:

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" role="img" aria-label="One trip with three catches" style="max-width:640px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:sans-serif;margin:.6rem 0">
  <rect x="10" y="75" width="175" height="60" rx="8" fill="#dbe9f6" stroke="#5b86b3"/>
  <text x="97" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="bold">Trip  trip_1</text>
  <text x="97" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12">Shimoni &#183; 5 Jan</text>
  <path d="M185 105 C 235 105 235 35 285 35"   fill="none" stroke="#5b86b3" stroke-width="2"/>
  <path d="M185 105 H 285"                       fill="none" stroke="#5b86b3" stroke-width="2"/>
  <path d="M185 105 C 235 105 235 175 285 175"  fill="none" stroke="#5b86b3" stroke-width="2"/>
  <rect x="285" y="15"  width="345" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#aaa"/><text x="300" y="40" font-size="13">Tilapia &#8212; 12 kg &#160;&#160;<tspan fill="#888">row 1</tspan></text>
  <rect x="285" y="85"  width="345" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#aaa"/><text x="300" y="110" font-size="13">Snapper &#8212; 5 kg &#160;&#160;<tspan fill="#888">row 2</tspan></text>
  <rect x="285" y="155" width="345" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fff" stroke="#aaa"/><text x="300" y="180" font-size="13">Octopus &#8212; 3 kg &#160;&#160;<tspan fill="#888">row 3</tspan></text>
</svg>
```

*One trip, three kinds of fish → three rows, all sharing `trip_id = trip_1`.*

The column **`n_catch`** writes that number down for you: it is **how many kinds of catch the trip
recorded**. You don't have to take it on trust — you can count the rows for each trip yourself. Press
**Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Count how many rows carry each trip_id.
table(example$trip_id)
```

The result shows `trip_1  3` and `trip_2  2`: three rows for the first trip, two for the second —
exactly matching the `n_catch` column. Counting how often something appears, like this, is already a
useful skill, and you will use it again later.

## Two kinds of columns

Now look across the columns. Once you see it, you cannot un-see it: the columns fall into **two groups**.
(Here the colours mark the **two kinds of columns** — not the trips as before.)

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex;gap:14px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin:.6rem 0;font-size:.95rem">
  <div style="flex:1;min-width:240px;background:#e6f4ea;border:1px solid #8cc6a0;border-radius:8px;padding:10px">
    <strong>About the trip</strong> <span style="color:#555">(same on every row)</span><br>
    <code>landing_date</code>, <code>gaul_2_name</code>, <code>gear</code>, <code>n_fishers</code>, <code>tot_catch_kg</code> &#8230;
  </div>
  <div style="flex:1;min-width:240px;background:#f3e8f7;border:1px solid #c79bd6;border-radius:8px;padding:10px">
    <strong>About each catch</strong> <span style="color:#555">(changes on each row)</span><br>
    <code>catch_taxon</code>, <code>catch_kg</code>, <code>length_cm</code>, <code>catch_price</code>
  </div>
</div>
```

Some columns describe the **whole trip**. They are the **same on every row of that trip**, because the
trip happened once: `landing_date`, `gaul_2_name`, `gear`, and `tot_catch_kg`, the **total** weight the
trip brought in.

Other columns describe **each catch on its own**, so they **change from row to row**: `catch_taxon`, and
`catch_kg`, the weight of that **one** kind of fish.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
This difference matters in real work. **`tot_catch_kg` is the whole trip's weight; `catch_kg` is one
fish's weight.** If you added up `tot_catch_kg` over every row, you would count the same trip several
times and get a number far too big. For a trip total you use `tot_catch_kg`; for a single catch you use
`catch_kg`.
:::

You do not need to memorise the columns — the next lessons introduce them one at a time. For now, just
hold the shape in your head: **rows are catches, rows group into trips, and every column is either about
the trip or about the catch.**

## Looking at your own data

You now know the shape. Let's load **your real landing records** — the same data you can open in the
**Data Download** tab — into the same kind of table. Press **Run**; the first time it may take a few
seconds.

{{< include _landings-data.qmd >}}

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| input:
#|   - landings_data
landings <- tryCatch(as.data.frame(landings_data), error = function(e) data.frame())

if (nrow(landings) == 0) {
  cat("Your data will appear here once you are signed in to the platform.\n")
} else {
  landings
}
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
This is your real data, and it has the **same shape** as the small example. Try typing the name of your
district, or a kind of fish, into the **search box** — or click a column heading to **sort**. Looking
around like this is the best way to get a feel for what you actually have.
:::

## How big is your data

Two simple questions help you get your bearings: **how many records** do you have, and **how many
columns** describe each one? Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
nrow(landings)   # number of records (rows)
ncol(landings)   # number of columns
```

The first number is how many catch records you hold — often many thousands. The second is how many
pieces of information are kept about each catch. This is far more than you could read by eye in a
spreadsheet, which is exactly why we use R: it can look through all of it for you in a moment, which is
what the next lessons will do.

## What each column means

Finally, let's see the columns by name. Press **Run** to list them:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
names(landings)
```

These are the headings in your table. Below is what the main ones mean, grouped the same way we saw
above. **Keep this nearby — it is the dictionary for your data.**

**Which trip a row belongs to**

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `survey_id` | The survey this record came from |
| `trip_id` | The fishing trip. Rows with the same `trip_id` are from the same trip |
| `n_catch` | How many kinds of catch that trip recorded |

**About the trip** (same on every row of the trip)

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `landing_date` | The day the catch was brought to shore |
| `gaul_2_name` | The district / area |
| `gear` | The fishing method (e.g. hand line, gillnet) |
| `vessel_type` | The boat used (e.g. dhow) |
| `n_fishers` | How many people were fishing |
| `trip_duration_hrs` | How many hours the trip lasted |
| `catch_habitat` | Where they fished (e.g. reef) |
| `tot_catch_kg` | Total weight of the whole trip, in kg |
| `tot_catch_price` | Total value of the whole trip |

**About each catch** (one row each)

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `catch_taxon` | The fish type, as a short FAO code (e.g. `SKJ` = skipjack tuna) |
| `scientific_name` | The fish's scientific (Latin) name |
| `length_cm` | The fish length, in centimetres |
| `catch_kg` | The weight of that catch, in kg |
| `catch_price` | The value of that catch |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Two things that look different in your real table

The **column headings** are the same as the small example, so what you practised will work here. But two
of the **values** look different, and it is worth knowing why before you go on.

- **The fish is a code.** In your real data `catch_taxon` holds a short code (for example `SKJ`), not a
  name. The `scientific_name` column gives its full name. We used everyday names such as *Tilapia* in
  the small example only to keep it easy to read.
- **`gaul_2_name` is the district, not the landing site.** The odd name comes from an international list
  of areas. Your table records the **district** a record belongs to, not the individual beach or jetty.
:::

## What you have learned

You can now read the shape of your data:

- a **row** is one catch — one kind of fish from one trip;
- rows belong together when they share a **`trip_id`**, and **`n_catch`** says how many a trip had;
- every column is either **about the trip** (the same on every row) or **about each catch** (different on each row);
- your real data has this same shape — just much bigger.

That is the foundation. In the next lesson you will start to **find the rows you need** — for example,
showing only the landings from your district, or only one month.
